k: What this is This is a complete set of topic guides for Pearson Edexcel A Level Mathematics (9MA0) — the whole two-year course, Year 12 and Year 13, Pure, Statistics and Mechanics. Every topic guide follows the same shape: 1. Why this topic exists — what problem it solves, and where it plugs into the rest of the course. 2. The ideas, built up in order — each new bit of machinery explained from the ground up, with the reasoning shown, not just the rule stated. 3. Worked examples — full solutions with the thinking written out, including the choices you have to make and why you make them. 4. Common mistakes — the specific, predictable ways students drop marks on this topic. 5. In the exam — what questions actually look like, what examiners want to see written down. 6. Practice questions — graded from routine to exam-standard, each with a full worked solution behind a toggle. How to actually use it (read this bit) Here is the uncomfortable truth about maths revision: reading a worked solution feels like learning and mostly isn't. When you read someone else's solution, your brain goes "yes, obviously, I could have done that." That feeling is called fluency illusion and it is the single biggest reason people walk out of a maths exam surprised by their own grade. So the rule for every practice question on this site: Attempt the question on paper, fully, to an answer , before you open the solution. If you get stuck, note exactly where you got stuck, then open the solution and read only until you're unstuck. Close it. Finish the question yourself. A workable routine for one topic: 1. Read the explanation sections properly once. Slowly. Pen in hand. 2. Cover each worked example's solution and try it first. Then compare, line by line. 3. Do the practice questions cold, on paper, timed roughly at 1.2 minutes per mark. 4. Mark yourself honestly against the solution. Write down every mark you dropped and why . 5. Come back to that topic 3 days later and redo the two questions you got wrong. This is the step everyone skips and it's the step that does the work. The four things that actually raise a maths grade - Spacing. Revisiting a topic after a gap beats re-reading it now. A topic done once and revisited three times over a term will outperform a topic hammered for four hours in one sitting. - Retrieval. k: The three papers Edexcel A Level Mathematics (9MA0) is assessed by three papers, all sat at the end of Year 13. There is no coursework and no non-calculator paper — a calculator is allowed in all three . Paper Content Length Marks Weight --- --- --- --- --- Paper 1: Pure Mathematics 1 Any pure topic from either year 2 hours 100 33⅓% Paper 2: Pure Mathematics 2 Any pure topic from either year 2 hours 100 33⅓% Paper 3: Statistics and Mechanics Section A: Statistics (50 marks)<br Section B: Mechanics (50 marks) 2 hours 100 33⅓% Two consequences that people underestimate: - Pure is two-thirds of the qualification. If you are short on time, pure is where the marks are. - Papers 1 and 2 are not split by year or by topic. Either paper can ask anything from the pure content. There is no "Paper 1 is Year 12". Everything is examinable everywhere. The grade boundaries typically land somewhere around 55–65% for an A, and around 80% for an A (the A is awarded on the overall total, not on a specific paper). Those move year to year — treat them as a rough map, not a target. Timing 200 marks of pure in 240 minutes, so 1.2 minutes per mark . A 6-mark question deserves about 7 minutes. If you're 3 minutes over on a question, leave it, mark it, come back. Students lose far more marks to unfinished papers than to wrong answers. What's in Year 12 vs Year 13 The split below is the standard Edexcel teaching order. The specification itself doesn't formally split AS from A2 content in the A Level, but this is how virtually every school sequences it, and it's how this resource is organised. Pure — Year 12 (AS content) Algebraic expressions · Quadratics · Equations and inequalities · Graphs and transformations · Straight-line graphs · Circles · Algebraic methods and proof · The binomial expansion · Trigonometric ratios · Trigonometric identities and equations · Vectors (2D) · Differentiation · Integration · Exponentials and logarithms Pure — Year 13 (A2 content) Proof by contradiction and partial fractions · Functions and modulus · Sequences and series · Binomial expansion for negative and fractional indices · Radians · Reciprocal and inverse trig functions · Addition formulae and the R-form · Parametric equations · Advanced differentiation · Numerical methods · Advanced integration and differential equations · Vectors (3D) Statistics Year 12: Sampling · Measures of location and spread · Data representation · Correlation and regression · Probability · The binomial distribution · Hyp

Why this topic exists A quadratic is any equation of the form with . They turn up everywhere: the height of a projectile, the area of a rectangle with a fixed perimeter, the intersection of a line and a circle, the condition for a tangent. More importantly, completing the square is one of the three or four genuinely powerful techniques in the whole of A Level pure. It's how you find a maximum or minimum without calculus, how you derive the quadratic formula, how you find the centre of a circle, and how you handle certain integrals in Year 13. Learn it properly now and it pays out for two years. --- 1. Solving quadratics Three methods, in the order you should consider them. (a) Factorising — fastest when it works This works because of the zero product property : if two things multiply to give zero, at least one of them is zero. That's the only reason factorising solves anything. . Do not divide both sides by — you've just thrown away the solution . Instead: or . Never divide an equation by a variable. Move everything to one side and factorise. (b) The quadratic formula — always works This is not in the formula booklet. Memorise it. (c) Completing the square — when you need more than the roots Covered in full below. Use it when the question asks for a maximum/minimum, a turning point, a range, or gives you the phrase "in the form ". --- 2. Completing the square The idea expands to . Why this topic exists Simultaneous equations answer the question "where do these two things meet?" — which is the same question as "where does this line cross this curve", "what's the break-even point", "when do these two particles collide". Inequalities answer "for what values is this true?" — and they are the standard finishing move for discriminant questions, domain questions, and anything involving "find the range of values of ". The single biggest source of lost marks in this topic is treating a quadratic inequality like a quadratic equation . There's a whole section on that below because it matters that much. --- 1. Simultaneous equations: two linears Two methods. Both fine. Pick based on the numbers. Elimination — scale the equations so one variable has matching coefficients, then add or subtract. Substitution — rearrange one equation for one variable, substitute into the other. Solution (elimination). To eliminate , make its coefficients and : multiply equation (1) by 3 and equation (2) by 2. Then check in the equation you didn't use for the substitution — checking in the one you used will confirm your answer even if you made an error, so it proves nothing. --- 2. Tangents and normals to curves (calculus), chords and radii of circles, regression lines in statistics, displacement–time graphs in mechanics — all straight lines. A typical 10-mark circle question is really four small questions from other topics stacked together.
